lesson.title: Heritability: How Much of a Trait Is In the Genes?
lesson.summary: Heritability measures what fraction of the variation in a trait across a specific population and environment is due to genetic differences among individuals, not how genetic any one individual's trait is.
lesson.body:
Heritability is one of the most commonly misunderstood ideas in biology, so it is worth being precise about what it does and does not mean. It is not a measure of how much of a single individual's trait comes from genes versus environment, an individual's phenotype is always the joint product of both. Instead, heritability is a statistic that applies to a population, describing what fraction of the variation among individuals in a trait, within a particular population living in a particular set of environments, can be attributed to genetic differences among those individuals, as opposed to differences in the environments they experienced. Heritability is expressed as a value between zero, meaning none of the variation traces to genetic differences, and one, meaning essentially all of it does.

This directly extends the idea of variation in populations from the previous chapter. That chapter established that populations contain heritable and non heritable sources of difference among individuals, mutation, recombination, but also things like diet, injury, or chance events during development. Heritability asks, of all that variation, how much specifically traces back to genotype. It also depends on the machinery covered earlier for how genes are actually transmitted, Mendel's law of segregation, which describes how the two alleles an individual carries separate during gamete formation so that each offspring receives one from each parent, and the chromosomal theory of inheritance, which established that genes are physically carried on chromosomes. Heritability builds on that transmission mechanism to ask, at the level of an entire population, how much of the variation we observe is actually being passed along generation to generation through that process.

A concrete example helps illustrate why context matters so much here. Within a population of people who all grew up with adequate and fairly similar nutrition, a large share of the variation in height between individuals traces back to genetic differences, so height would have relatively high heritability in that setting. But if you instead compared two different populations, one that experienced significant childhood malnutrition and one that did not, most of the average height difference between those two populations would be environmental, not genetic. Same trait, very different heritability, depending entirely on which population and which environments are being compared. Heritability is not a fixed property of a trait for all time, it can change if the environment changes.

This matters enormously for what comes next. For natural selection to change a population across generations, the variation that gives some individuals a survival or reproductive edge has to be heritable. If an advantageous trait is purely the result of environment, with no genetic basis, it cannot be passed to offspring, and selection has nothing to accumulate from one generation to the next.
